common_name: Springhigh Southern Highbush Blueberry (Ultra-Early Low-Chill Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant in late winter to early spring in acidic, well-drained soil; Springhigh has a very low chill requirement of around 150-200 hours and is among the earliest-ripening southern highbush blueberries, well suited to zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun, and pair with another early-blooming southern highbush variety for best pollination and fruit set. Developed by the University of Florida's blueberry breeding program, Springhigh was selected for an unusually low chilling requirement that lets it flower and fruit reliably in the mild winters of the Deep South, where many northern blueberry types fail to break dormancy evenly. It ripens very early in the season, often the first blueberry to color up in the garden, giving growers a jump on the market and on fresh eating alike. Keep soil consistently moist during bloom and fruit development, since southern highbush types have shallow root systems that dry out quickly in sandy Gulf Coast soils.

common_name: Dorman Red Raspberry (Heat-Tolerant Deep South Trailing Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil and train the long trailing canes onto a wire trellis, since Dorman Red does not stand upright like northern raspberries.

directions: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun and trellis the long, trailing canes on a two-wire support, since this variety sprawls rather than growing upright. Selected in the Deep South specifically to withstand summer heat that kills most raspberry cultivars outright, Dorman Red is one of the few raspberries that reliably fruits in zone 8-9 gardens where standard northern types decline within a year or two. It produces a single crop in late spring on second-year canes, with medium-sized, tart-sweet red berries that are excellent for preserves as well as fresh eating. Prune out spent floricanes immediately after harvest to make room for the current season's new growth, and keep roots mulched to buffer summer soil heat.

common_name: Mars Seedless Grape (Cold-Hardy Disease-Resistant Blue Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring in well-drained soil; Mars is self-fertile, compact, and well suited to a small arbor, patio trellis, or single-wire fence rather than a full commercial vineyard trellis.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor. Bred at the University of Arkansas breeding program and released in the 1970s, Mars combines good disease resistance with genuinely seedless, blue-black berries and a sweet, fruity, slip-skin flavor reminiscent of Concord but milder. Its compact vine habit and strong resistance to common grape diseases make it far easier to grow without a heavy spray program than European wine grapes, especially in humid climates. Prune hard each winter to a few renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

common_name: Champanel Grape (Extremely Vigorous Pierce's Disease-Resistant Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring in well-drained to occasionally wet soil; Champanel is extremely vigorous and tolerates poor drainage and Pierce's disease pressure far better than most grapes, making it a strong choice for humid Gulf South sites where other grapes struggle.

directions: Plant in average to poorly drained soil in full sun on a strong arbor or high-wire trellis able to support very vigorous growth. Bred by Texas grape pioneer T. V. Munson in the late 1800s from a cross of the wild Vitis champinii with an American labrusca-type grape, Champanel is renowned for tolerating conditions that kill most grape vines outright, including heavy soil, occasional flooding, and Pierce's disease, a bacterial illness common in the humid South. The large, dark purple-black berries are tart and seedy, better suited to juice and jelly than fresh eating, but the vine's toughness makes it a dependable arbor and shade grape where other varieties fail. Prune to a permanent framework each winter to manage its rampant growth.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

common_name: Conquistador Grape (Disease-Resistant Black Juice and Jelly Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring in well-drained soil on a sturdy trellis; Conquistador carries strong Pierce's disease tolerance from its Munson-lineage breeding, making it a reliable choice for humid Gulf South vineyards and home arbors.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor. Developed from breeding lines descended from T. V. Munson's disease-resistant Texas grape stock, Conquistador produces vigorous vines with strong tolerance to Pierce's disease and other conditions that limit grape growing in hot, humid regions. The medium-sized black berries are tart and well suited to juice, jelly, and homemade wine rather than fresh eating out of hand. Because vines are vigorous and productive, prune firmly each winter to a permanent set of cordons and thin fruit clusters if growth becomes crowded, which improves air circulation and reduces fruit rot in humid weather.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
